To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the traction forces of migrating neutrophils are dependent on substrate stiffness and chemotactic gradient strength, and that the magnitude of traction forces correlates with directional motion only when the neutrophils experience an ideal chemotactic gradient.

(1) neutrophils generate traction forces that are spatially organized in response to chemotactic gradients; (2) neutrophils are capable of moving directionally on compliant substrates; (3) the relationship between the magnitude of traction forces and the chemotactic response depends on substrate stiffness and the magnitude of the chemotactic gradient; and (4) inhibition of Rho-associated kinase or β(2)integrin signaling greatly reduces rearward traction forces.

the magnitude of traction forces generated by neutrophils correlates with directional migration on stiff substrates and under ideal chemotactic conditions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the traction forces of neutrophil migration on hydrogel substrates are dependent on both substrate stiffness and the strength of the chemoattractants, and that the magnitude of traction forces and the direction of migration are not always correlated.
